bequest

bih-KWEST · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Bequest is a gift of money or property left to someone in a will.

The library's new wing was funded by a bequest from a retired teacher who died last spring.

Example

In her will, Great-Aunt Rosa left the beach cottage to her niece -- a bequest that changed the young woman's life.

The cottage was property passed on through a will after Rosa's death -- exactly what a bequest is: not just any gift, but one delivered by a will.

How bequest sits among its neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

legacy

legacy: money or property handed down after someone's death

inheritance

inheritance: what you receive from someone who has died

Antonyms

debt

debt: money that is owed to someone

disinheritance

disinheritance: being deliberately cut out of a will

How Strong Is It?

gift → bequest → endowment

gift vs. bequest

gift vs. bequest: A gift can be handed over at any time, for any reason -- a bequest is specifically given through a will, after the giver has died.

endowment vs. bequest

endowment vs. bequest: An endowment is a large gift, often a bequest, meant to fund an institution permanently -- it emphasizes lasting support rather than the will itself.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of bequest.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — be-: about; thoroughly (Old English)

root — -quest: to say, declare (from cwethan, the root of 'quoth') (Old English)

Put it together: Be- ('thoroughly') + -quest ('to declare'): a bequest began as something formally declared -- spoken into a will -- which is why it means property passed on after death.

Use the root in a new word: bequeath: The composer chose to bequeath his piano to the conservatory where he had studied.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Bequest is formal, legal vocabulary -- the world of wills, estates, museums, and universities. The thing left behind is the bequest; the act of leaving it is to bequeath.
